coredata.dc:description: Bisphenol S (BPS) and 4-hydroxyphenyl 4-isoprooxyphenylsulfone (BPSIP) have been used as substitutes for bisphenol A (BPA) owing to increased regulation of BPA in plastics. In this study, long-term toxicity tests of BPS and BPSIP were performed using Daphnia magna and Moina macrocopa. The predicted no-effect concentration (PNEC) of BPA, BPS, and BPSIP were derived by the assessment factor (AF) method and the species sensitivity distribution (SSD) method. An ecological risk assessment was performed based on the measured environmental concentrations of BPA in surface water worldwide and the derived PNECs. The chronic NOEC of D. magna was 2.5 mg/L for BPS and 0.5 mg/L for BPSIP, and that of M. macrocopa was 0.03 mg/L for BPS and 0.1 mg/L for BPSIP. The PNECAF was generally one order of magnitude less than the PNECSSD, and the PNEC of BPS was 10 times lower than that of BPA. The hazard quotients of BPA and BPS exceeded 1, indicating that concentrations in ambient water conditions could pose a potential risk to aquatic organisms. Since the use of alternative compounds is increasing, further monitoring data of the water environment and chronic toxicity in various aquatic organisms appears to be necessary.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Bisphenol S (BPS) and 4-hydroxyphenyl 4-isoprooxyphenylsulfone (BPSIP) have been used as substitutes for bisphenol A (BPA) owing to increased regulation of BPA in plastics. In this study, long-term toxicity tests of BPS and BPSIP were performed using Daphnia magna and Moina macrocopa. The predicted no-effect concentration (PNEC) of BPA, BPS, and BPSIP were derived by the assessment factor (AF) method and the species sensitivity distribution (SSD) method. An ecological risk assessment was performed based on the measured environmental concentrations of BPA in surface water worldwide and the derived PNECs. The chronic NOEC of D. magna was 2.5 mg/L for BPS and 0.5 mg/L for BPSIP, and that of M. macrocopa was 0.03 mg/L for BPS and 0.1 mg/L for BPSIP. The PNECAF was generally one order of magnitude less than the PNECSSD, and the PNEC of BPS was 10 times lower than that of BPA. The hazard quotients of BPA and BPS exceeded 1, indicating that concentrations in ambient water conditions could pose a potential risk to aquatic organisms. Since the use of alternative compounds is increasing, further monitoring data of the water environment and chronic toxicity in various aquatic organisms appears to be necessary.

ce:section.ce:para: Considering its widespread application and significant adverse effects on human health, bisphenol A (BPA) has been regulated by the European Union (2011), US Food and Drug Administration (2010), and Health Canada (2009). In response to this restriction, BPA analogues such as bisphenol S (BPS) and bisphenol SIP (BPSIP) have been introduced to replace BPA in various consumer products. BPS and BPSIP have a common structure of two hydroxyphenyl functionalities like BPA (Lee et al., 2018). In recent years, BPS has frequently been detected in human urine and blood samples (Thayer et al., 2016), personal care products (Liao and Kannan, 2014), thermal paper (Liao et al., 2012), as well as surface water samples (Yang et al., 2014). BPSIP concentrations in thermal receipt paper ranged from 3.4 to 13.2 mg/g (Goldinger et al., 2015); however, reliable detection is difficult in the surface water environment. As the use and detection frequency of BPA substitutes increase, so does the importance of investigating the effects of BPS and BPSIP on aquatic organisms.

Currently, the chronic ecotoxicity data of BPS and BPSIP is extremely limited compared to that of BPA. In algae, invertebrates, and fishes, the half maximal effective concentration (EC50) or median lethal concentration (LC50) of BPS have been reported at 106 mg/L (U.S. EPA, 2015), 55–100 mg/L (Chen et al., 2002; U.S. EPA, 2015), and 155–500 mg/L (Moreman et al., 2017; U.S. EPA, 2015), respectively. BPSIP has far less ecotoxicological data than BPS, and acute toxicity of BPSIP has been reported at 2.22 mg/L for Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata, 13.4 mg/L for Daphnia magna, and 18.8 mg/L for Oryzias latipes (ECHA, 2019). Therefore, research on the chronic toxicity of BPS and BPSIP will be necessary to evaluate their ecological risk and to establish appropriate management plans.

Water quality criteria (WQC), environmental quality standard (EQS), and predicted no effect concentration (PNEC) of toxic chemical are important metrics in ecosystem protection and ambient water quality management (Xing et al., 2014). According to the European Communities (2011), PNEC can be determined by three methods: the assessment factor (AF) method, the species sensitivity distribution (SSD) method, and model ecosystem method. The AF method derives the PNEC value by using an appropriate AF (from 10 to 1000) to the lowest chronic no-observed-effect concentration (NOEC). The SSD method, which is currently used as the most common method in deriving WQC, plots cumulative probabilities of log-transformed toxicity values for aquatic species with multiple taxonomic groups and trophic levels, and calculates hazardous concentration for 5% of the species (HC5). The criterion continuous concentration (CCC) using the SSD method were reported to be 0.46–7.50 μg/L for BPA, 54.0 μg/L for BPF, and 26.4 μg/L for BPAF in aquatic environments (Guan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018). The deterministic AF method could be overly-conservative compared to the predictive SSD method owing to its high level of uncertainty (Xing et al., 2014). To date, PNEC does not cover most of the bisphenol analogues such as BPS and BPSIP.

Several organizations have provided guidance on the number of species necessary for carrying out the SSD method; however, the data quantity and quality have significant effects on the HC5. In general, it is recommended to have at least 10 long-term NOEC datasets (preferably more than 15) covering at least 8 taxonomic groups (European Communities, 2011). However, those criteria are too strict to apply, so different criteria have been proposed. For example, the US EPA recommends a minimum of 8 datasets from 3 phyla and 8 classes (U.S. EPA, 1985), and the Australian and New Zealand Environment Conservation Council recommends at least 5 species from 4 different taxonomic groups (ANZECC, 2000). The Netherlands recommends using 4 or more taxonomic groups for SSD statistical extrapolation (RIVM, 2001). To accurately assess the ecological risk caused by BPA, BPS, and BPSIP, it is important to obtain sufficient chronic toxicity data, especially on growth and reproductive effects on aquatic organisms.

In this study, supplementary acute and chronic toxicity tests for BPS and BPSIP were performed using two freshwater invertebrates, i.e., D. magna and Moina macrocopa, the latter being an indigenous species in Asia. Toxicity data were collected from the literature and used to derive PNECs by AF and SSD methods. Finally, the ecological risk was evaluated by estimating hazard quotient (HQ) based on the measured environmental concentrations (MECs) of BPA and BPS in surface waters and the derived PNECs.

Bisphenol S (CAS number: 80-09-1) and bisphenol SIP (CAS number: 95235-30-6) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). To ensure that exposure levels remained constant, we analyzed the BPS and BPSIP in the exposure media using a UHPLC system, Nexera (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan), with an API 4500 triple quadrupole mass spectrometry system (AB SCIEX, Ontario, Canada). Water samples were collected from each treatment group at least three times. After filtering the sampled water using a 0.2 μm syringe filter, an internal standard (BPS 13C12) was added. BPS and BPSIP were separated using an UHPLC C18 column (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). The electrospray ionization conditions for the analysis and linearity of the calibration curves are shown in Tables S1–S2, and Fig. S1. The limit of detection was 0.24 ng/mL for BPS and 0.26 ng/mL for BPSIP. There was high agreement between nominal and measured concentration; so, we used the nominal concentration in this study (Table S3).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Maintenance and exposure of D. magna and M. macrocopa
ce:section.ce:para: D. magna and M. macrocopa were maintained in M4 media at 21 ± 1 °C and 25 ± 1 °C, respectively, under a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod. Crustaceans were fed daily with Chlorella vulgaris (AquaNet, Gyeongnam, Korea), and the medium was changed at least three times a week. The water temperature, conductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen, alkalinity, and hardness were monitored daily.

The D. magna (21 d) and M. macrocopa (7 d) chronic toxicity tests were conducted as outlined in Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) test guidelines 211 (OECD, 2012) and recommended by Oh and Choi (2012), respectively. Concentrations for long-term exposure were determined based on the preliminary acute toxicity test results, (i.e. 48 h acute EC50 for BPS and BPSIP, according to the OECD test guideline 202 (OECD, 2004)). For D. magna chronic toxicity tests, 10 neonates per group were exposed to BPS (0, 0.62, 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10 mg/L) and BPSIP (0, 0.06, 0.12, 0.25, 0.5, 1 mg/L). For M. macrocopa chronic toxicity tests, concentrations were 0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.11, 0.33, 1 mg/L for both BPS and BPSIP. The endpoints were survival of parent animal, first day of neonate production, number of neonates per parent animal, number of neonates per brood, and growth (in case of D. magna). Following the Euler-Lotka equation (Heugens et al., 2006), the population growth rate (r) was calculated. If the parent animal died or turned out to be male, those organisms were excluded from the analysis. Feeding, water change frequency, and water quality parameter checking resembled those in culture.

To calculate PNEC of BPA, BPS, and BPSIP, ecotoxicity data from the literature or the results of the present study were used. The acute toxicity data (EC50 and LC50) and chronic toxicity data (NOEC and EC10) were obtained from the ECHA Information on Chemicals database (https://echa.europa.eu/information-on-chemicals) and the PubMed engine (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/). The endpoints related to immobilization, mortality, growth, and reproduction were collected. The PNEC was derived from the most sensitive toxicity data point and an appropriate AF following European Communities (2011). Different AFs were applied following the availability of acute and chronic toxicity data for three different trophic levels, i.e., algae, invertebrates, and fishes (Supplementary data, Table S4).

For BPA and BPS, which is possible to collect the minimum of five species from at least four taxonomic groups following the RIVM (2001) and ANZECC (2000) protocol requirements and to fit the data to parametric distribution, the SSD approach was applied. The PNEC calculation using the SSD method was performed in four stages: toxicity data screening, distribution model selection, SSD curve fitting, and HC5 and PNEC calculation to quantify the ecological risk (Gao et al., 2014). If there was a variety of toxicity data for the same species, a geometric mean was calculated. The log-normal distribution was adopted for SSD curve fitting, and the probability distribution fitted to the datasets used for the calculation of HC5 were checked with the Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit test and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. From the SSD, the HC5 value was further derived using the software program SSD generator provided by US EPA (https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2017-10/ssd_generator_v1.xlsm). The PNEC value was determined by dividing HC5 by the appropriate safety factor (ECB, 2003), which varies between 1 and 5. A safety factor of 2 and 5 was selected for BPA and BPS, respectively, based on the amount and the quantity of toxicity data.

Hazard quotients of BPA and BPS were calculated by dividing the MEC by the PNEC. The MEC data was collected from the studies on surface water, drinking water, ground water, and effluents conducted globally in literature. If the HQ value is greater than 1, ecological impact is considered for the given bisphenols.

Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS® version 18.0 K, for Windows® (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett's test was used to examine differences between control and treatment groups. Before performing ANOVA, the normality of distributions and homogeneity of variances were checked using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Levene's test, respectively. Values were considered statistically significant when p was less than 0.05.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Toxicity of chronic exposure in crustacean
ce:section.ce:para: The 48 h immobilization EC50 of D. magna was 87 mg/L of BPS and 14.2 mg/L of BPSIP, and that of M. macrocopa was 20.1 mg/L of BPS and 9.82 mg/L of BPSIP (Table S5). In D. magna exposed to BPS and BPSIP for 21 d, no adverse effects of survival and reproduction were observed at the test concentration (Fig. 1 ). However, the body length of D. magna was significantly reduced when exposed to 5 and 10 mg/L of BPS and 1 mg/L of BPSIP (Fig. 1). Population growth rates of D. magna exposed to BPS and BPSIP were greater than zero (Fig. 1).

M. macrocopa exposed to BPS for 7 days showed a significant decrease in survival at 1 mg/L (Fig. 2 ). First day of reproduction was significantly increased at 0.1 mg/L BPS and 1 mg/L BPSIP (Fig. 2). The number of young per female, one of the most sensitive endpoints related to the reproduction, was significantly decreased with treatments of 0.1 mg/L of BPS and 0.3 mg/L of BPSIP (Fig. 2). In M. macrocopa exposed to BPS, number of young per brood was significantly decreased at 0.3 mg/L (Fig. 2). NOEC values for reproduction of BPS and BPSIP were 0.03 mg/L and 0.1 mg/L, respectively (Table S5).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Derivation of PNEC by AF method and SSD method
ce:section.ce:para: A sample size of chronic toxicity data (NOEC or EC10) was 17 species from 11 taxonomic groups for BPA and 6 species from 5 taxonomic groups for BPS, and this size was fulfilled the technical requirements of SSD model suggested from the Netherlands (RIVM, 2001) and Australia (ANZECC, 2000). Fitting the distributions to the toxicity data revealed that the log-normal distribution was the best method. The log-normal distribution was accepted when p < 0.05 according to both the Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit test and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Based on the SSD models of chronic toxicity, HC5 data were 22.8 μg/L for BPA, 4.03 μg/L for BPS (Table 1 and Fig. 3). Based on the safety factor of 2 for BPA and 5 for BPS, the PNECSSD was derived as 11.4 μg/L for BPA and 0.81 μg/L for BPS (Table 1).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ecological risk assessment of BPA and BPS
ce:section.ce:para: Using the most sensitive toxicity data (Table S5) and the maximum MECs worldwide or in Korea (Table S6), HQ values were calculated (Table 2 ). Based on the PNEC value derived from the AF method, HQs for BPA and BPS were 17.5 and 72, respectively (Table 2). Based on the PNEC value derived from SSD method, HQs for BPA and BPS were calculated at 2.45 and 8.9, respectively (Table 2).

Bisphenol A and BPS were detected as high as 5.03 μg/L in Yeongsan river and 0.042 μg/L BPS in Han river, respectively (Table S6). The Korean HQs for BPA and BPS were 3.14 and 0.42, respectively, using the conventional AF method (Table 2). Based on the PNEC value derived from SSD method, HQs for BPA and BPS were 0.44 and 0.05, respectively (Table 2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Toxicity of chronic exposure in crustacean to BPS and BPSIP
ce:section.ce:para: Although BPS and BPSIP are important alternatives to BPA, these compounds have not been assessed for ecological risk because of a lack of environmental toxicity data. In this study, chronic toxicity tests of D. magna and M. macrocopa were carried out to fill the toxicity data gap by deriving PNEC for BPS and BPSIP. Values for the acute toxicity test were consistent with the EC50 reported by previous researchers; the 48 h D. magna EC50 for BPS and LC50 for BPSIP were reported to be 55–100 mg/L (Chen et al., 2002; U.S. EPA, 2015) and 13.4 mg/L (ECHA, 2019), respectively.

Chronic exposure to BPS and BPSIP adversely affected growth and reproduction of D. magna and M. macrocopa. The NOEC value of D. magna exposed to BPS (2.5 mg/L) was consistent with the results of a previous study (2.7 mg/L; ECHA, 2019). Interestingly, the NOEC of BPS in M. macrocopa (0.03 mg/L) was lower than the value of BPSIP (0.1 mg/L). A previous study also reported that BPS appeared to have more profound effects on egg production in zebrafish than did BPSIP (Lee et al., 2018). A plausible explanation of the differences could be their chemical structures; the extent to which the isopropyl ether at the end of the phenolic rings in BPSIP may regulate toxicity (Lee et al., 2018).

Compared to D. magna, M. macrocopa (a freshwater water flea living in Korea, and in Asia, more broadly) was more sensitive to both compounds. Oh and Choi (2012) showed that chronic three-brood toxicity tests using M. macrocopa is faster and more cost-effective than D. magna chronic toxicity tests. For this reason, the M. macrocopa chronic toxicity tests was frequently performed to evaluate the ecological risk in regions where M. macrocopa is native (Jang and Ji, 2015; Kwak et al., 2018). Several studies have simultaneously examined the chronic toxicity of the two species and found that M. macrocopa was more sensitive than D. magna when exposed to naproxen (Kwak et al., 2018) and perfluorinated compounds (Ji et al., 2008). Further studies will be needed to characterize environmental pollutants that are more sensitive to M. macrocopa. The results of chronic BPS and BPSIP exposure tests for M. macrocopa can be used for ecological risk assessment in Korea surface water.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison between the AF method and SSD method in deriving PNEC
ce:section.ce:para: PNEC values derived using the AF approach are conservative, easy to use, and applicable when there is a lack of ecotoxicological data. However, the AF method has a high degree of uncertainty because extrapolation from the individual level to the population level is dependent on the toxicity data of the most sensitive species and a specific AF value (Gao et al., 2014; Grechi et al., 2016). The resulting PNEC value for BPA was one order of magnitude lower than that reported in other studies [50 μg/L (Tišler et al., 2016) and 5 μg/L (Liu et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017)] or greater than that reported by Selvaraj et al.(2014), i.e., 0.1 μg/L. Liu et al.(2017) and Yan et al.(2017) derived a PNEC of 55 μg/L for BPS, a value about 500 times greater than that reported in our study (0.1 μg/L), which was derived based on the most sensitive NOEC observed in D. rerio (Naderi et al., 2014). The PNEC of the BPSIP (10 μg/L) was derived based on the reproduction NOEC observed in M. macrocopa, with an AF of 10. The main reason for the observed difference of PNEC values is considered to be the different NOEC value and the AF used for deriving the PNEC values.

The SSDs for BPA and BPS were constructed by plotting the cumulative probability of log-transformed toxicity threshold values for aquatic species with different sensitivities, including multiple trophic levels and various taxonomic groups. The HC5 value calculated for BPA in the present study (22.8 μg/L) was similar to others reported: 18 μg/L (Staples et al., 2008), 15 μg/L (Wang et al., 2018), and 2.59–7.74 μg/L (Guo et al., 2015). To account for the remaining uncertainties in the estimated HC5, we applied an additional AF of 2 to HC5 for BPA to derive a PNECSSD value. Although the AF was applied differentially in each study, the PNECSSD for BPA, 11–71 μg/L (Staples et al., 2008) and 7.5 μg/L (Wang et al., 2018) were not significantly different from ours (11.4 μg/L). The PNECSSD for BPS was 0.81 μg/L, with 6 long-term toxicity datasets from 5 taxonomic groups. Although the number of chronic toxicity datasets used in this study meets the minimum requirements suggested by RIVM (2001) and ANZECC (2000), the number of toxicity datasets for BPS is less than that suggested by the European Communities (2011). Considering that the sufficient number of toxicity data could increase the reliability of calculating HC5 and PNEC values, both the size and quality of the dataset should be increased, especially in the case of BPS.

The SSD method is more reliable and predictable than the AF method (Gao et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2010) because it focuses on the toxicity effects of the whole community by using the full toxicity dataset. Therefore, the SSD approach should be used to evaluate ecological risks whenever sufficient data are available (Wheeler et al., 2002). In the present study, PNECAF of BPA and BPS were generally 7–8 times lower than PNECSSD. Previous study also showed that AF-derived PNEC value of 1.6 μg/L was 10 times lower than the SSD-derived PNEC values of BPA (11–71 μg/L) (Staples et al., 2008). These results suggest that the AF method can be used as a screening tool for the ecological risk assessment of new chemicals including BPA alternatives with scarce ecotoxicological data; however, it is better to derive the predictive PNEC with the SSD method if there is sufficient toxicity data. Even though the SSD method focuses on toxicity effects on the investigated community, this approach could ignore the ecological interactions between species (Grechi et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2010). Further studies are needed to derive PNEC of BPA and its alternatives using experimental ecosystems (e.g., microcosm and mesocosm) or field enclosure studies.

Several studies comparing the PNEC of BPA and its substitutes showed that alternative compounds such as BPAF and BPF could be more toxic than BPA (Liu et al., 2017; Tišler et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017). In the present study, the calculated PNECAF of BPSIP was greater than that of BPA; however, the PNECAF of BPS was 10 times lower than that of BPA. Previous studies reported that the effects of BPS on reproduction are no less than the effects of BPA (Ji et al., 2013; Naderi et al., 2014). Exposure to environmentally relevant concentrations of BPS (0.5 μg/L) resulted in decreased egg production in the F0 generation, and delayed hatching and increased rates of malformation in offspring (Ji et al., 2013). Given the importance of the effects on reproduction and the continuous release of BPS, further information about possible adverse effects on various species are needed.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ecological risk assessment of BPA and BPS
ce:section.ce:para: The ecological risk of BPA and BPS was assessed by comparing the MEC worldwide with the PNEC derived in this study. When applying the maximum MEC value reported for BPA (28 μg/L in Czech Republic; Heisterkamp et al., 2004) and BPS (7.2 μg/L in India; Yamazaki et al., 2015), the HQs of BPA and BPS in surface water worldwide were greater than 1, indicating that both bisphenols could cause risk to aquatic life. While we applied the maximum MEC value reported for BPA in the Yeongsan river, Korea (5.03 μg/L; Park et al., 2012), and BPS in the Han river, Korea (0.042 μg/L; Yamazaki et al., 2015), the HQ was less than 1, except HQ of BPA using PNECAF value. Since the MEC in the Yeongsan river is close to the maximum allowable PNEC of BPA, the potential risk of BPA in this area should be considered in the future. Given the assumption of the increased concentration of BPS in ambient water, the risk to the aquatic ecosystem is expected to be higher. In the future, risk assessment of BPA alternatives should be improved using the most recent monitoring data and PNECSSD derived for various aquatic organisms.
